Power & Grid.why: Transformers, switchgear, gas turbines, fuel cells, SMRs — where the buildout actually hits the physical world. Transformer lead times of 30–40 months and PJM interconnection queues over 8 years make this the single most binding constraint in the stack.

Compute & Silicon.why: Where capital is most concentrated and most exposed. The HBM hybrid-bonding monopoly (BESI/ASMPT) and the EDA duopoly (Synopsys/Cadence) are durable. Merchant AI accelerators and frontier labs are not — post-Groq, the exit math is brutal.

Materials & Chemicals.why: Quiet near-monopolies. GOES electrical steel (Cleveland-Cliffs is the sole North American producer), EUV photoresists, high-purity silicon wafers, InP / GaAs substrates for photonics, and titanium alloys for gas-turbine generators that now power AI campuses.

Connectivity & Photonics.why: Inter-region and intra-rack bandwidth. Subsea triopoly, multi-decade dark-fiber IRUs from hyperscalers, and the CPO / silicon-photonics transition that copper interconnect cannot scale past.

Construction & Labor.why: Skilled electricians, mechanical contractors, transmission specialists. A 1 GW campus needs 3,000–4,000 electricians at peak; the IBEW pipeline cannot supply at AI cadence. MEP contractors now turn down work — pricing power is structural.

Cooling & Thermal.why: GB200/GB300 racks at 120+ kW exceed air-cooling limits. Microsoft made liquid cooling the default for its Maia accelerators; Nvidia Vera Rubin is designed for 45°C hot-water cooling. Air→liquid retrofit cycle is forced, not optional.

Fab & Test Equipment.why: The picks and shovels behind every chip. Litho tools (ASML for EUV, AMAT/LRCX for deposition and etch, KLA for inspection) print the transistors; test handlers (Teradyne, AEHR) prove the wafers and packages survive. A narrow oligopoly the entire foundry universe runs through — and the part of the stack still being repriced.

Software & Apps.why: The demand layer. Enterprise AI integration is where model output becomes revenue, and where the trillion-dollar capex bill ultimately gets paid for. ServiceNow leads the front-office integration race; multiple-X upside remains even with the name in the open.
